title_en: The Passion of Perpetua and Felicity
author: Perpetua, Saturus, and the Redactor
addressee: fellow Christians, addressed as "brothers and little children" who will hear or read the account
occasion: New visions and martyrdoms have occurred and the editor believes they should be written down and read in church like older examples, so that God is honored and faith is strengthened rather than supposing divine grace worked only in the past.
argument: The editor argues that recent prophecies, visions, and martyrdoms carry the same authority as ancient ones because the Spirit was promised for the last days and God still acts for believers and against unbelievers. Perpetua's prison diary then shows her resolve under her father's pleas and interrogation, and her visions reveal that her coming death is an ascent to paradise and a contest against the devil that she will win. Saturus's vision confirms this by showing the martyrs carried to a garden of light, welcomed in white robes before God's throne, where they find Optatus and Aspasius separated and sad and asking for reconciliation, and Perpetua speaks with them in Greek to reconcile them. Felicitas's answered prayer for early childbirth so she can die with the others, the group's defiance over dress and witness in the arena, and her own going from blood to blood to be washed in a second baptism present their suffering as victorious witness for the church to celebrate.

outline.move: Editorial prologue argues new examples of grace, prophecy, and visions must be recorded and read like old ones.
Editor introduces the arrested catechumens, Perpetua's family and child, and hands narration to Perpetua.
Perpetua recounts arrest, baptism, prison hardships, her father's early pleas, condemnation by Hilarianus, and her ladder-to-paradise vision.
Perpetua recounts prayer and two visions for her dead brother Dinocrates, moving from suffering to refreshment.
Perpetua recounts her father's last anguished plea at the prison, with no vision in this section.
Perpetua recounts her eve-of-contest vision of defeating the Egyptian with a heavenly trainer's branch.
Saturus recounts being carried by angels to a rose garden and luminous throne room, then reconciling the sorrowful Optatus and Aspasius.
Editor links the narratives, noting Secundulus's prison death and Felicitas's answered prayer for early childbirth before the games.
Editor narrates the final meal, entry to the arena, scourging, the men's encounters with leopard, bear and boar, the cow attack on the women, and death by throat-cutting that seals their victory.

cast.name: Perpetua
cast.who: 22-year-old noble married mother and catechumen who writes the prison diary and dies in the arena.

cast.name: Felicity
cast.who: Fellow slave/servant of Revocatus, pregnant when arrested, who gives birth in prison and is martyred with Perpetua.

cast.name: Revocatus
cast.who: Catechumen arrested with the group and later exposed to leopard and bear.

cast.name: Saturninus
cast.who: Catechumen arrested with the group who asks for all the beasts.

cast.name: Secundulus
cast.who: Catechumen who dies in prison before the arena.

cast.name: Saturus
cast.who: Their fellow Christian who voluntarily surrendered himself for their sake, because he had built them up, writes his own vision, and dies consoling the soldier Pudens.

cast.name: Dinocrates
cast.who: Perpetua's seven-year-old brother who died disfigured by illness and appears in her intercessory visions.

cast.name: Hilarianus
cast.who: Procurator acting for the dead proconsul who interrogates and condemns them to beasts.

cast.name: Tertius and Pomponius
cast.who: Blessed deacons who bribe guards and minister to the prisoners.

cast.name: Pudens
cast.who: Prison officer turned sympathizer who receives Saturus's bloodied ring.

cast.name: Optatus
cast.who: Bishop seen in Saturus's vision separated and sad alongside Aspasius, with both asking the martyrs to reconcile them.

cast.name: Aspasius
cast.who: Priest and teacher seen with Optatus needing reconciliation.

voices.speaker: Anonymous redactor/editor
voices.how_marked: third-person framing, hortatory prologue and epilogue, verbs of arranging and supplementing

voices.speaker: Perpetua
voices.how_marked: first-person prison narrative introduced as written in her own hand and feeling, with inquit and postulaui / uideo vision reports

voices.speaker: Saturus
voices.how_marked: first-person vision introduced as published and written by himself, opening Passi, inquit

imperial birthday gladiatorial and beast show where sentence is carried out
water baptism and martyrdom or blood as a second cleansing wash
supernatural opponent figured as dragon, serpent, Egyptian, and cow
the Christian community edified by reading and possessing the Spirit's gifts

scripture: The work cites Joel's last-days Spirit promise in the Acts form, not from a psalter, so there is no Psalm-numbering issue here; render ancient book and divine names in modern Bible form and cite Joel 2:28-29 / Acts 2:17-18 in modern chapter-verse form with a note that the Latin follows the author's wording.
uncertain: Identity of the redactor and later association with Tertullian cannot be established from this text alone.
Exact year and legal setting beyond Geta Caesar's birthday games and named Hilarianus and deceased Minucius Timinianus.
Whether Greek phrases and liturgical cries record verbatim speech or editorial shaping.
Precise medical, topographical, and ritual details behind Dinocrates's illness, prison transfers, dress coercion, and gate names.

_unresolved_facts.claim: the group's defiance over dress and witness in the arena
